performers: Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau, baritone; Berlin Philharmonic; Rudolf Kempe, conductor
question: What changes in a repeated melody when “gone out” becomes “gone ahead”?
intro: The parent first imagines that the children have merely gone for a walk, then that they have gone ahead to another world. Mahler repeats and alters a short stanza pattern, keeping the accompaniment moving beneath each attempted reassurance.

sections.label: First stanza · only gone out
sections.mNote: horn and string lines frame the first reassurance

sections.label: Second stanza · reassurance repeated
sections.mNote: the vocal outline returns with changed instrumental support

sections.label: Last stanza · gone ahead
sections.mNote: the repeated idea leads towards a larger final rise

cues.title: Movement beneath reassurance
cues.text: Horn and strings shape the opening above a steady lower pulse. Listen for the short moving figures in the cellos: the accompaniment does not become motionless just because the poem speaks reassuringly.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Song IV, printed p. 48; the opening cello figure, horn line and harp/bass pulse are visible. This describes the opening passage rather than a single attack.

cues.title: A small verbal change
cues.text: The poem begins by imagining that the children have simply gone out and will return. Its last stanza changes that thought: they have gone ahead, and the parent will eventually follow them.
cues.evidence: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/kindertotenlieder/kindertotenlieder-lied-4-oft-denk-ich-sie-sind-nur-ausgegangen/ German text: ausgegangen becomes vorausgegangen. This is an overview of the poem, not a subtitle timed to a sung word.

cues.title: The reassurance starts again
cues.text: The second stanza recovers the first stanza’s melodic outline, but the accompaniment is not copied note for note. Compare the renewed vocal phrase with the instrumental figures that keep the line moving.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed p. 52, rehearsal 3. Both reports mark a change at 0:54 and renewed activity near 1:06. The stanza boundary is estimated, not word-aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A song published separately
cues.text: The piano-vocal version of this fourth song appears as a supplement to the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik on 10 May 1905. The complete cycle’s first editions follow later that year.
cues.evidence: https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/KtL/KtL.htm Chronology: separate publication on 10 May 1905, then full-score, part and vocal-score publication in August.

cues.title: Variation within repetition
cues.text: In the last stanza, follow the returning vocal shape against the cello and woodwind lines. Repetition makes the changed words audible as a revision of the earlier thought, not the start of a different song.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed p. 56, rehearsal 5. The report marks 1:50, then a rise from the quiet 1:55 window into the 2:02 change. These features support passage-level placement only.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Before Mahler’s own loss
cues.text: Mahler completes the cycle in 1904. His daughter Maria dies in 1907; these songs are settings of Rückert’s bereavement, not a memorial composed after Maria’s death.
cues.evidence: The composition range is documented in https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/KtL/KtL.htm; Mahler’s 1907 loss is recorded in the Mahler Foundation’s cycle introduction (https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/kindertotenlieder/kindertotenlieder-introduction/). The dates establish chronology, not a prophecy.

cues.title: The final rise subsides
cues.text: The strongest late swell gives way to a short, quiet ending. Compare its rise with its withdrawal: the repeated stanza has accumulated more force before the instruments settle.
cues.evidence: The analysis identifies 2:40 as the loudest five-second window; level falls from −9.0 dB at 2:50 to −21.5 dB at 2:55 and −44.5 dB at 3:00. No final chord is identified from the machine key estimate.

transitions.title: The stanza returns in a thinner texture
transitions.how: After a brief slowing, the vocal outline begins again at the restored pace. Clarinet and bassoon writing comes forward while much of the string texture briefly falls away. The repeated phrase is recognisable, but the altered accompaniment makes the renewed reassurance an active attempt rather than a mechanical repeat.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed p. 52, rehearsal 3. Both reports identify a boundary at 0:54; the exact first word of the stanza is unaligned.

transitions.title: The same melody carries a changed claim
transitions.how: The third stanza retains the earlier melodic family while harp pulse and moving cello figures support it differently. Woodwinds and divided strings sustain and answer the voice. The score’s instruction not to hurry keeps the repeated material connected to its first appearance, even as the final ascent gives the thought a greater range.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed pp. 56–59, rehearsal 5 onwards. The 1:50 change and quiet 1:55 window supply the approximate stanza boundary. The rise is measured later, around 2:35–2:45.

source.title: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, full score (C. F. Kahnt, plate 4460)
source.locator: Song IV, printed pp. 48–59; passage-level scoring, not an instantaneous list of sounding parts. Timings are provisional score proportions checked against the recording’s level changes; no bar alignment or aural verification.

timeline.note: Opening passage: horn melody, moving cellos and string lines above harp and pizzicato bass.
The first vocal stanza develops the opening material amid changing wind and string support.
At the renewed stanza, clarinet figures and bassoon support emerge from a thinner texture.
Last-stanza passage: cello movement and the harp pulse continue beneath sustained wind and string lines.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
